A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained content can be matched despite appendix renumbering and journal reformatting.

before.justification: v3 reports original curve-fitting, manifold-propagation, sphere-classification, MNIST, and computational-timing experiments in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experiments and adds empirical false-negative measurements for distance-thresholded overlap detection in Appendix D.5 and Figure 11.

M1.justification: Proposition C.4 adds an explicit residual-network adaptation using affine factors Q_J W + M to incorporate skip connections. The existing linear-programming, union-find, and quotient-distance procedures remain unchanged; residual-network experiments are not reported.

E1.justification: Empirical coverage remains nonlinear curves, D-I–D-III, sphere classification, MNIST, and synthetic timing tests. The new threshold study reuses the sphere datasets. The added XOR and architecture constructions are theoretical examples.

E2.justification: The comparisons retain Euclidean persistent homology for nonlinear curves and the reproduced Naitzat et al. (2020) pipeline for manifold propagation. No comparison method is added or removed from these experiments.

E3.justification: Appendix D.5 introduces a protocol testing distance thresholds at the 1st, 5th, 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles against the 100th-percentile reference, using a defined overlap-matching false-negative measure. The original splits, training settings, and model configurations in Tables 1–3 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Figure 11 measures missed overlaps as the distance threshold varies, supplementing the existing runtime sensitivity analysis. The nonlinear-curve failure examples, MNIST occupancy analysis, and orthogonal-initialization comparison are retained.

E5.justification: The existing model counts, mean-and-standard-deviation reporting, and Bonferroni-corrected Kruskal–Wallis tests are retained. The new threshold analysis uses the ten sphere models and adds error-barred results without introducing a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Figure 11 adds false-negative curves showing substantial errors at low distance percentiles and approximately zero errors at the 50th and 75th percentiles. The matched original plots retain their results, including Figure 3 despite its redraw.

T1.justification: Theorem B.2 now explicitly excludes singleton classes when accounting for non-injectivity. Theorem B.5 removes the general contractibility assumption and adds a contractible-fiber argument invoking Vietoris–Begle. v4 also formalizes the coarse equivalence relation and adds propositions on single-layer overlaps, XOR constructions, overlap counts, and residual networks, plus computational-complexity reasoning.

C1.justification: The central quotient-homology and slower-topological-simplification claims remain. The abstract drops v3’s assertion that the training study varies network width and depth, narrowing its description of the empirical contribution. The new conclusion largely restates existing core claims.

C2.justification: New Section 5.2 substantially develops computational tractability, distinguishing worst-case, expected, and populated-region scaling. Other additions discuss interactions between homological error types, memorization, and rank-versus-overlap expressivity. Section 3.2 also strengthens the convexity-applicability assertion for sufficiently large networks, although Appendix B still describes the supporting argument as heuristic.

D1.justification: v4 adds a Code Availability statement identifying the work’s repository, clarifies the distance criterion for skipping linear programs, and documents the new threshold-analysis procedure in Appendix D.5. Existing hyperparameter tables, software information, and hardware disclosure are retained.

R1.justification: v4 adds Goujon et al. (2024), Karmarkar (1984), Spanier (1966), and Stephenson et al. (2021) to support complexity, topology, and memorization discussions. The established positioning relative to persistent homology and polyhedral-decomposition research remains.

P1.justification: Terminology and explanations are refined, and separate Conclusion, Code Availability, and Examples sections are added. Former Proposition B.6 moves to Proposition C.1, with subsequent appendices relettered. Most existing prose and the main narrative order remain intact.

P2.justification: v4 adds the XOR diagrams in Figures 4–5, the expressivity construction in Figure 6, and the false-negative plot in Figure 11. Figure 3 is redrawn with layer labels and clearer caption guidance. Journal formatting changes typography, headers, page dimensions, and figure placement; other existing plots and tables are retained.

improvement.justification: Compared with v3, v4 improves precision through singleton accounting and the narrower B.5 assumption, quantifies the previously acknowledged risk of missed overlaps, and supplies code-access information. These improve assessability. The gain is limited by mathematical imprecision in the additions, including the inconsistent description of Proposition C.3 as a lower bound in Section 5.4 and an upper bound in its proof.
